character_and_relationship_context: Lakshmi Devi is a village woman whose hands are never still. She walks six kilometres from her village to the river bend and back, carrying a blue plastic bucket in one hand and a bamboo staff in the other. The bucket holds samples—water from hand pumps, from shallow wells, from the ditch where children sometimes play. She wraps each sample in a length of old sari to keep it cool, and on the return leg she stops at every pump to wipe the rim with a clean cloth before filling her container. Her movements are slow but precise; she has done this every day for eighteen months. At the university laboratory, students tease her gently: “Lakshmi-ma’am, you bring us cleaner water than we can collect ourselves.” She laughs, but does not slow down. She was born in the same village, the youngest of five daughters. Her first memory is of the communal tap—a rusted iron pipe that ran for two hours in the morning and two hours at dusk. She carried a brass lota to school, then a plastic jerrycan after she married and moved to her husband’s home. Her husband, a weaver, died of kidney failure when their youngest child was twelve. The doctors said it might have been the water. Lakshmi does not know for sure, but she remembers the way his ankles swelled, the smell of the village pond in the dry season. Her children now live in the city—a son who sells mobile phones, a daughter who works in a call centre. They call every Sunday and beg her to move. She tells them she has work to do. “The university people need me,” she says, though really it is the other way around. She has learned to read the colour chart for arsenic strips, to record coordinates in a thick notebook with a pencil tied to a string. She argues with the younger field assistants about which wells to prioritise. They want statistical coverage; she wants every hand pump that a child might drink from. She believes, with a clarity that surprises even herself, that water can be made clean. Not through prayer alone—she still lights a lamp every morning—but through patience, through walking, through testing each drop one by one. When people ask why she bothers at her age, she says, “I am not too old to carry water. I have carried it all my life. Now I carry the truth of it.” In relation to others, she has a cordial but punctuality-sensitive relationship with the van driver, who once threatened to leave without her when she was ten minutes late. The unknown woman is a young mother from a neighboring hamlet; Lakshmi has seen her drawing water here before but never spoken. When she sees a hand pump used by children, she has often interrupted her route to test it, even if it meant arriving late to the lab. She has also, on occasion, skipped a test to keep the van driver from honking again, because she values his help.
objective_situation: Lakshmi is at the river bend collecting a sample from a shallow well when she hears the university van honk twice from the main road—the agreed signal that they are leaving in ten minutes. As she straightens up, she notices a woman she does not recognize drawing water for her children from a nearby hand pump that Lakshmi has not tested this month. The woman smiles and offers her a drink. The stated alternatives are that Lakshmi can either walk quickly to the van without explaining, or take five minutes to test the pump with her arsenic strip and risk making the driver wait.
state_and_available_memories: She has just walked six kilometres carrying a bucket of samples and feels a familiar ache in her knees, but she is still steady on her feet. Her mind is calm, focused on the task; she is not yet tired enough to hurry without reason. Immediate memories: the woman’s smile and the offer of water remind her of her own daughter as a child, who once drank from a pump that later tested positive for arsenic. The honk of the van recalls a previous occasion when the driver left without her, forcing her to walk twelve kilometres back to the village.
name: Lakshmi Devi
scenario_title: The University Van is About to Leave
